thread.title: Tech Cos. Like IBM Could See Tax Hike: Bernstein | Investopedia

author: Shoshanna Delventhal
title: Tech Cos. Like IBM Could See Tax Hike: Bernstein | Investopedia
text:
Tech Cos. Like IBM Could See Tax Hike: Bernstein By Shoshanna Delventhal | January 18, 2018 — 10:06 AM EST 
The stock market continues its rally into 2018 as investors cheer the passing of the recent GOP tax bill, which is set to slash the corporate tax rate and incentivize overseas cash repatriation . While the tax overhaul has been deemed a major win for corporate America, one team of analysts on the Street warns that it may actually end up increasing the tax rate for big tech companies, specifically those offering services and software. (See also: The Biggest Corporate Winners From Trump Tax Deal. ) 
The tax plan, passed in December, could spell bad news for tech titans, notably legacy enterprise software provider International Business Machines Corp. ( IBM ), according to analysts at Bernstein. Analysts Toni Sacconaghi and Daniel Chen wrote a note to clients forecasting IBM’s normalized tax rate to rise from just 15% to “closer to 20 percent or more.” They noted that IBM may have to make a one-time accounting charge due to write-down of deferred tax assets. Other “losers” include companies with low tax rates and some service companies. Sorry Not Sorry 
The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, which reduces the corporate tax rate by 14% to 21%, may seem like a major win for the market. Yet while U.S. corporations are in no way complaining, many America's most powerful companies were already enjoying a tax rate lower than 35%. Four of the five biggest companies in the S&P 500 scored a less than 35% effective rate over the past 11 years, according to data from FactSet. Apple Inc. ( AAPL ) paid at a 26.1% rate, Microsoft Corp. ( MSFT ) at 23.8%, Google parent company Alphabet Inc. ( GOOG ) at 21.1% and Amazon.com Inc. ( AMZN ) at 31.5%. Facebook Inc. ( FB ) paid a 40.3% rate over the same period. 
Recently, analysts at Goldman reduced tech from overweight to neutral weight, writing that under the plan, health care and tech should see the smallest gains. "Tech has the lowest effective tax rate of any sector [24%] and would benefit the least under the various proposals," analysts wrote before the bill passed. "Although Tech has the highest expected sales growth and profit margins, it also has the highest risk from tax reform, valuation, and government regulation," wrote the Wall Street bank. (See also: Trump Tax Plan ‘As Good as It Gets’ for US Banks. )
